newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan tea prices seen strong in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan tea prices seen strong in 1997.

text.p: Sri Lankan tea prices are expected to remain strong this year, although off last year's record highs, on continuing good demand, industry officials said on Wednesday.
"Prices have been picking up since January and will remain strong, but we're not sure if we will reach the extremely high levels which we saw late last year," a Tea Board official said.

Tea prices soared to record highs late last year mainly because of strong winter demand for the distinct low grown teas from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), Sri Lanka's biggest tea market, and the Middle East.

The Colombo auction average price for calendar 1996 rose to a record 103.88 rupees ($1.81) per kg from the previous year's high of 72.21 rupees per kg. The sale average in 1994 was 65.12 rupees per kg.
In January this year, the auction average price fell below 100 rupees per kg but it has picked up since then.
The Indian Ocean island is the world's biggest tea exporter with about 18-20 percent market share and exported a record 244 million kg last year, up from 240 million kg in 1995.

"I don't think tea prices will maintain the same high levels of 1996 this year but they will still be attractive. Last year we had a real boom," said Sudath Munasinghe, tea director at brokerage John Keells Ltd.
"Still, prices are going to be better than in previous years and will be remunerative for the producer," he added. "They are not going to be loss-making like the years before 1995."
Industry officials said it was still too early to say if Sri Lanka could maintain the same crop level as last year's record harvest of 258.4 million kg, because of drought.
"The drought has caused crop intakes to drop sharply, not just from higher elevations, but in low growns in particular," brokers Forbes and Walker said in a recent report.

Last year's increase in production -- up five percent from the 245.9 million kg in 1995 -- came from low grown teas, which make up half the crop. Sri Lankan teas are categorised according to factory elevation -- high, medium and low.

"We're a bit unsure of the crop this year," the Tea Board official said. "During the latter part of 1996 there was a severe drought which is still continuing. The crop depends on the weather. If in April-May there is still drought then the crop will fall."
Munasinghe of John Keells said he felt the increase in the crop during rainy months could offset the deficit during dry periods.

"In 1996 we had drought and power cuts but still had a record crop," he said. "It could be the same this year too. When the rains start we will get a good crop. We can catch up. February was a bad month - fairly dry. But last week there was some rain."
The privatisation of the island's tea plantations had also helped increase the crop, industry officials said.

"With better agricultural practices and the use of more fertiliser, even this year there could a better crop," said Munasinghe. "Estates which were bought by the private sector are going to pump in money."
